about.title: Fillmore Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Fillmore's economy runs on agriculture, packing operations, and the small businesses that line A Street and Ventura Street, and workers in these settings face real risks — equipment accidents, falls, repetitive strain, and vehicle-related incidents on routes like Rt 126. Most workplace injuries in California are handled through workers' compensation, which pays medical care and partial wage replacement regardless of who was at fault. But that system doesn't cover everything, and it doesn't apply at all when someone outside your employer — a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver — caused or contributed to the harm. In those cases, a separate third-party injury claim may be available alongside your workers' comp benefits. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect injured workers in Fillmore with an independent attorney who can look at the details of your injury, your job, and how it happened, then explain what options might realistically apply to you.

whyChoose.title: Why Fillmore Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We Help You See Beyond the Comp System
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but if a third party contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible. An attorney can help identify whether that applies to your case.

items.title: We Understand the Reporting Clock
items.desc: California law generally requires reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Missing that window can complicate your claim, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation Is Built Into the Law
items.desc: It's illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting an injury or pursuing a claim. An independent attorney can help you understand your rights if you're worried about your job.

items.question: Can I file a claim if I was hurt driving for work near Fillmore's Route 126?
items.answer: Possibly. Workers' comp typically covers injuries during work travel, but if another driver caused the crash, that driver's insurance may be a separate source of recovery. An attorney can review the crash details to see what applies.

items.question: What if my employer says my injury doesn't qualify for workers' comp?
items.answer: Employers don't have final say over whether a claim qualifies. If you believe you were wrongly denied, an independent attorney can review the denial and explain your options, including appeal processes.

items.question: Is there a deadline to bring a third-party claim after a work injury?
items.answer: Yes, third-party injury claims in California generally carry a two-year deadline from the date of injury. That's separate from workers' comp reporting rules, so it helps to get both timelines clarified early.
